newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU ministers agree new Swiss compromise on transit.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers agree new Swiss compromise on transit.

text.p: EU transport ministers agreed on Thursday a revised package of measures to offer Switzerland in bilateral talks intended to resolve trans-Alpine freight traffic problems related to a Swiss ban on heavy trucks.

Ministers "broadly backed" a report by European Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock intended to answer the conflicting demands of the Swiss, who hold to their 28-tonne limit on trucks, and neighbours Austria and France, which are angry about the traffic flowing over on to their trans-Alpine routes.
But ministers's support came with some additional demands.
"We are very anxious to secure both access and transit rights for EU 40-tonne trucks," Irish Transport Minister Alan Dukes told a news conference after the meeting.

Dukes, whose country holds the EU presidency until the end of the year, said truck charging proposals sketched out by ministers would help Switzerland raise the cash for a long-term solution to the transit problem, namely the building of a rail tunnel to carry increased freight flows through the country.
Switzerland and the EU's 15 countries have spent months discussing closer ties in a range of areas such as research, trade in processed farm products and free movement of people.

Most areas have been resolved but problems remain in liberalising road and air transport. The EU wants immediate access to Swiss roads for its 40-tonne trucks while Berne wants the set up of a differentiated charging system penalising dirtier trucks in return for giving up its 28-tonne maximum-weight limit.

Kinnock's chief aide Philip Lowe told reporters that Swiss demands now were linked with the EU's own efforts to revise its existing "Eurovignette" tax system to favour cleaner trucks, with low axle weights, over dirtier trucks carrying the higher axle loads which cause greatest damage to roads and bridges.
He said the revised Eurovignette rules would provide the legal basis for agreeing a trans-Alpine road charging system.

A Kinnock paper presented earlier suggested the EU demand of Berne free access for its 40-tonners on Swiss roads from the year 2005 subject to an unspecified maximum charge-per-kilometre to apply also to French and Austrian Alpine routes to Italy.

Switzerland, in return for access to EU road freight markets and a guarantee clause in the deal, would develop its promised, combined road/rail transit capacity to offer trucks an alternative route across the Alps, Kinnock said.
Ministers also want a reciprocal guarantee clause in the event of Switzerland's failure to build extra rail capacity.

In parallel, the EU would raise its current "Eurovignette" truck charge -- covering Belgium, Denmark, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Germany and Sweden -- in line with inflation rates since 1993 and would weight the fee to favour cleaner trucks and two, three and six-axled vehicles over four and five-axled ones.

It was unclear after the meeting whether a revision of the Eurovignette rules would help to end Austria's row with the Commission over its Brenner pass truck tolls, some of which exceed $200 per trip depending on travel time and truck type.
Vienna says the tolls reflect the environmental damage caused by trucks but the Commission deems them illegally high.

Germany, France, Britain, Portugal and Austria had earlier appeared in favour of a proposal to classify the Brenner pass as an environmentally sensitive route qualifying for a special tariff but opposition from Italy prevented a clear decision, officials told reporters.
